rules.message: document.write/writeln breaks HTML parsing once the document has loaded (blocked under many CSP/PWA setups) and can clobber the page. THE DOM CALLS DO NOT INSERT WHERE OR WHEN `document.write` DID, AND TWO OF THE THREE DIFFERENCES FAIL WITHOUT RAISING. `document.write` splices its string into the token stream at the parser's current position, so there is no node to append to yet: a call reached from `<head>` meets a `document.body` that is still `null`, and one that ran mid-body has to be given an explicit parent and a position that the markup around it may never have named. A `<script src=...>` written that way is parser-blocking — the parser stops, fetches it and runs it before the next tag — whereas a script element you create and append loads ASYNCHRONOUSLY unless `async` is set to false, so code that used to find the library defined now runs first and reads `undefined`. And `textContent` is not a substitute for markup at all: it prints tags as characters, so whatever this call was writing as HTML appears as text. Read what the call actually writes before replacing it — a plain string is a one-line change, a script tag is an ordering change, and markup aimed at the parse position needs a container that exists at the moment it runs. Build DOM nodes (or set textContent) instead. Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-no-document-write-ok:`.

A `postMessage(..., '*')` call sends the payload to whatever origin currently holds the window at delivery time — an opener swap, an embedding iframe/parent change, or a same-window navigation to a different origin all qualify, so a `'*'` targetOrigin does not authenticate the recipient and can leak the payload to an attacker-controlled origin. Pass the exact intended origin (a literal `https://...` string, or a validated same-origin check) instead of `'*'`. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a genuinely non-sensitive broadcast payload) with `// zzop-postmessage-wildcard-ok`.

A `.innerHTML`/`.outerHTML` assignment, `insertAdjacentHTML(...)` call, or JSX `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` prop whose value is not a plain no-interpolation string literal — this is the classic DOM XSS sink: whatever ends up in that string is parsed and executed as HTML/script by the browser. A SANITIZER-PASSAGE veto keeps the rule off values that were already cleaned: the finding is dropped only when a sanitizer-shaped call is the ENTIRE value — `escape*`/`sanitize*`/`validate*`/`purify*` (optionally method-qualified, so `DOMPurify.sanitize(x)` counts) or a name carrying `Safe`/`Sanitized`/`Escaped`/`Purified` ANYWHERE in it, so `jsonLdSafe(x)` and `markdownToSafeHTML(x)` both count. Only that ADJECTIVE half of the vocabulary is position-free; the verb half is still start-anchored, so a verb-final `htmlEscape(x)` is NOT vetoed and still fires. `Unsafe` is kept out by spelling alone — the token carries a capital `S`, which `unsafeHTML` and `render_unsafe_html` never produce. WHOLE-VALUE is ENFORCED, not merely claimed: the veto consumes the call's own argument list and then requires the value to END (`;`, `,`, a closing `)`/`}`, or end of line), so every shape that leaves attacker-controlled text OUTSIDE the sanitized call still fires — `escapeHtml(title) + rawUserHtml` (concat), `sanitizeSvg(a) ? raw : other` (ternary), `sanitize(x).replace(/a/, evil)` (method chain), and a template literal that interpolates an escaped fragment into an `href=` attribute. Escaping a fragment is not the same as sanitizing the HTML around it. `JSON.stringify(x)` is deliberately NOT in this vocabulary: JSON encoding escapes only `"`, `\` and control characters, so `<`, `>`, `&` and `/` pass through verbatim — `__html: JSON.stringify(data)` breaks out of its ``, which is exactly why a `jsonLdSafe`-style wrapper (`JSON.stringify(x).replace(/` seen from inside `Preview`); every one of those shapes still fires, and closing it needs local/interprocedural dataflow that a line-scan matcher does not have. SCOPE NOTE on the PROP spelling: it is a residual only where the caller set is CLOSED — a component private to the tree, whose call sites can all be read. On a component its package EXPORTS, the caller set is open-ended and a `svg: string` prop type promises nothing about sanitization, so the finding there is CORRECT rather than a limitation: the remedy is to sanitize inside the component or to take a branded sanitized-HTML type, not to suppress. Residual 3 — LINE AND NESTING BOUNDS, and this one always errs toward MORE findings: a sanitizer call broken across lines, or one whose arguments nest parentheses more than one level deep (`escapeHtml(a(b(c)))`), is not provably whole-value on a single line and therefore fires. Note: `security/taint-flow` already covers these same sinks, but only when a request-derived source (body/query/params/headers) co-occurs in the SAME function, and only in `.ts`/`.tsx` files; this rule needs no such source — component props/state passed down through the tree are the far more common XSS carrier in FE code — and it also covers `.js`/`.jsx`. A SANITIZER IS AN ALLOW-LIST, SO IT DELETES WHATEVER IT WAS NOT TOLD TO KEEP, AND THE PAGE STILL RENDERS: nothing throws and nothing is logged, so the loss arrives as an embed that is simply gone, a link that stopped opening in a new tab, or a block that lost the attribute it was styled by. The lists are library defaults rather than a standard, and they are narrower than authored content usually is — `sanitize-html` ships a short tag list holding no `iframe`, `svg`, `video` or `form` and grants attributes only to `a` and `img`, so `class`, `style` and `id` come off the elements it does keep, while DOMPurify keeps far more and still drops `iframe` and the `target` attribute until they are added back. The plain-text route is not selective at all: `textContent`, jQuery `.text()`, Vue `{{ }}` and an escaped template form print markup as characters, so a stored `bold` reaches the reader as that literal text rather than as bold type. Settle which of the two this value is BEFORE the edit — where it is text the substitution is right and costs nothing, and where it is markup somebody authored, sample what this sink receives today, configure the allow-list against that sample, and keep the configuration in one place instead of per call site. Use `textContent` for plain text, or a vetted HTML-sanitizer library (e.g. DOMPurify) if HTML must genuinely be inserted — never assign unsanitized dynamic content into an HTML sink. Suppress a vetted case (value is provably sanitized upstream) with `// zzop-unsafe-html-sink-ok`.

A `javascript:` scheme URL executes arbitrary script the moment the link is clicked or the resource is loaded — the browser treats everything after the scheme as code, not a navigation target. AN http(s)-ONLY SCHEME TEST REJECTS MORE THAN THE ATTACK, AND MOST OF WHAT IT REJECTS IS ORDINARY: a same-site path (`/settings`), a query-only or fragment-only href, and the `mailto:`, `tel:`, `blob:` and `data:` targets a page uses for contact links, generated downloads and inline previews all fail a check spelled as `startsWith('http')`. Resolve the candidate against the document's base URL first and compare the resulting `protocol` against the schemes this app actually uses, so a relative href keeps working. The literal findings are their own case: `javascript:void(0)` and `javascript:;` are placeholder hrefs, and DELETING the attribute is not neutral — an anchor with no `href` is not a link, so it leaves the tab order, loses its focus ring, its `:link`/`:visited` styling and its pointer cursor, and stops announcing itself as a link, while swapping in `#` adds a history entry and jumps the page to the top. Where the element was only ever a click target, make it a `button` and move the handler onto it; where it is a real destination, put that destination in the `href`. Never construct a link/image/script target from a `javascript:` scheme; if the target must be dynamic, validate the scheme against an http(s) allowlist before using it. Note most bundlers/linters miss this. Scope limit: this rule only catches the LITERAL `javascript:` form written directly in source (`href="javascript:..."`, `.href = 'javascript:...'`, `setAttribute('href', 'javascript:...')`); a dynamic `href={someUrl}`/`.href = someUrl` whose value only turns out to be a `javascript:` URL at runtime is a different, harder taint-tracking class this rule does not attempt — see `location-assign-dynamic` for the closest DSL approximation of a dynamic-value sink.

A navigation sink (`location`/`location.href` assignment, or `location.assign(...)`/`location.replace(...)`) whose value is not a plain literal — an open-redirect or DOM-XSS surface if that value is influenced by the URL, a query param, or any other untrusted input, since the browser will navigate to (or in some cases parse-and-execute) whatever string ends up there. THIS RULE READS THE ASSIGNMENT'S OWN LINE AND RESOLVES NO NAMES, which is its own false-positive vector twice over. (1) When the `=` closes the line and the value sits on the continuation line below it (`window.location.href =`, then `data.redirectUrl ?? ...`), nothing on the value side is read at all — the receiver spelling is the entire evidence, so a wrapped assignment of a plain literal is reported here while the same literal written on one line is not. (2) The literal veto below needs the literal SPELLED AT THE ASSIGNMENT: a path literal bound to a name a few lines up and then assigned through that name (`const gettingStartedPath = "/getting-started"`; … `window.location.href = gettingStartedPath`) is reported exactly like a request-derived value, and the veto written to silence it never sees the binding. Neither is a gap a pattern can close: `line-scan` has no field that resolves a name to the value it holds, so both are disclosed rather than fixed. Validate the target against an allowlist (a known set of paths, or a same-origin check) before navigating. Boundary note: `security/open-redirect` covers the SERVER-side sink (`res.redirect(req.*)`); this rule covers the CLIENT-side navigation sink instead — the two never overlap. A literal URL string (`location.href = '/login'`, `location.href = "https://x.com"`) stays silent, as does a bare `const location = ...` declaration (e.g. React Router's `useLocation()` result). An INTERPOLATING TEMPLATE is not a plain literal and does fire (`` location.href = `${base}${query}` ``), but only where nothing pins the destination ahead of the first `${`: a template opening with a path or a scheme (`` `/app/${id}` ``, `` `https://${host}/x` ``) stays silent for the same reason the `base + '/path'` concat does, and the protocol-relative `` `//${host}/x` `` is missed with it. The template arm also requires the receiver to be SPELLED (`location.href`, or anything under `window.`): a bare `` location = `...` `` is not matched, because an unqualified `location` holding a template is far more often a local of that name (a meeting-location string, a `useLocation()` result) than the global. A `base + '/path'` concat where a string path-literal (`+ '/...'`) is appended is also vetoed: prepending a base pins the origin/path, so the trailing dynamic segment is a path component, not a scheme/origin sink (the common `getBaseUrl() + '/admin/' + filename` idiom) — but a query-suffix concat (`base + '?next=' + q`) or a bare dynamic value (`location.href = returnUrl`) still fires, since neither pins the destination. Also receiver-aware like `no-document-write`: only the bare global `location`/`window.location` is flagged, so an arbitrary domain object's own `.location` field (`user.location = ...`, `job.location.assign(...)`) is never matched. Since 2026-08-21 the UNQUALIFIED global additionally requires WHITESPACE before its `=` (`location = url`, not `location=url`); `location.href` and anything spelled through `window.` are unaffected and match with or without. That is a notation rule, not a vocabulary one, and it is what separates an assignment in formatted source from two things that merely look like one: a `window.open` FEATURE STRING (`` `toolbar=no, location=no, directories=no, …` ``, where `, location=n` is lexically an assignment to the global — it was 1 of the 2 findings this rule produced on koel BEFORE the whitespace requirement, and koel now reports 1, the real `location.assign(url)` sink in `resources/assets/js/services/authService.ts`) and a JSX PROP (`<Route location={location} />` — 6 of them across grafana). Neither is code assigning to the global, and no formatter writes an assignment without spaces. The cost, stated rather than measured away: an unqualified `location=url` written without spaces — legacy or hand-minified source — is now missed, while `window.location=url` is not, because the receiver spelling is itself evidence that this is the global rather than a key in a string or a prop name. Across this engine's corpus every no-space match was one of the two shapes above and none was a real sink, so the loss is a shape the corpus does not contain rather than a shape it contains and forgives.

A jQuery HTML-insertion method (`.html()`, `.append()`, `.prepend()`, `.after()`, `.before()`, `.wrapAll()`) called with a non-literal argument — the same DOM-XSS surface as `.innerHTML`, since jQuery parses a string argument to these methods as HTML and inserts it. Known imprecision: a DOM-element/jQuery-object argument (e.g. `.append($('
'))`) is lexically indistinguishable from an HTML string argument, so it also fires there — accepted as the FP-safe subset's price of admission, kept as a warning rather than critical. Settle which of the two this value is BEFORE the edit — where it is text the substitution is right and costs nothing, and where it is markup somebody authored, sample what this sink receives today, configure the allow-list against that sample, and keep the configuration in one place instead of per call site. Use `.text()` for plain text, or sanitize the string first (e.g. DOMPurify) if HTML must genuinely be inserted. Boundary note: distinct from `unsafe-html-sink`, which covers the native `.innerHTML`/`.outerHTML`/`insertAdjacentHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` sinks, not jQuery's own API surface. Gated on the file mentioning `jquery` or a `$(` call so a same-named method on an unrelated object (e.g. a custom `.append()`) doesn't fire in a non-jQuery codebase.

Vue's `v-html` directive renders its bound expression as raw HTML — the Vue analog of React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — so it is XSS if the bound value is influenced by user input (a route param, API response, user-submitted content, etc.). A markdown-to-HTML render call (`marked`, `markdown-it`, `md.render`, `remark`, `showdown`) whose output reaches an HTML sink (`innerHTML`/`outerHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`/`v-html`) in the same function/component with no sanitizer (`DOMPurify`/`sanitize`/`sanitizeHtml`/`xss`) anywhere in that same span — markdown renderers emit raw HTML by default, so piping their output straight into an HTML sink is stored XSS (a real corpus shape: `marked(article.body)` rendered via a sibling `v-html`). A SANITIZER IS AN ALLOW-LIST, SO IT DELETES WHATEVER IT WAS NOT TOLD TO KEEP, AND THE PAGE STILL RENDERS: nothing throws and nothing is logged, so the loss arrives as an embed that is simply gone, a link that stopped opening in a new tab, or a block that lost the attribute it was styled by. Settle which of the two this value is BEFORE the edit — where it is text the substitution is right and costs nothing, and where it is markup somebody authored, sample what this sink receives today, configure the allow-list against that sample, and keep the configuration in one place instead of per call site. THE RENDERER-OPTION ROUTE IS THINNER THAN IT READS: `marked` deprecated and then removed its own `sanitize` option and hands the job to a dedicated sanitizer, and the options that do survive elsewhere — `markdown-it` ships `html: false` by default — work by ESCAPING the embedded HTML, which is the visible-text outcome above rather than an allow-list you can widen. Run the output through DOMPurify/sanitize-html, or enable the renderer's own sanitize option if it has one. This is method-scan (co-occurrence within one function/component span): if the render call and the HTML sink live in different spans (e.g. render happens in a composable, the sink in the consuming component) this rule will not co-fire.
